title: Are power markets fit for purpose? | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Vistra's Stacey Doré argues on Energy Gang that headline data-centre load forecasts are inflated by speculative and duplicative interconnection queue requests, that existing generation can serve most near-term growth for the vast majority of hours, and that the true bottleneck is interconnection speed rather than megawatts. Amy Myers Jaffe counters that the live issue is cost allocation, since the fast-rising part of household bills is transmission and distribution rather than wholesale generation.

insights.claim: Some of the most eye-catching forecasts for new US electricity demand are overstated because the same speculative projects file duplicative requests across multiple interconnection queues, inflating the apparent pipeline.
insights.speaker: Stacey Doré, Vistra
insights.so_what: If queue-based demand numbers are double-counted, capacity-price and turbine-order theses built on them are overbuilt; watch for queue-deduplication reforms as the catalyst that resets forecasts.
insights.quote: some of the most eye-catching forecasts for new demand are overstated by speculative projects and duplicative queue requests
insights.locator: The discussion starts with a challenge to the dominant narrative around load growth

insights.claim: The existing US generation fleet already has enough capacity to serve most near-term load growth for the vast majority of hours in the year, making the shortfall a narrow peak-hour problem rather than an energy-volume problem.
insights.speaker: Stacey Doré, Vistra
insights.so_what: Reframes the investment need from bulk new baseload toward peak-shaving tools, which favours storage, demand response and uprates over greenfield gas.
insights.quote: the grid already has enough existing generation to serve most near-term growth for the vast majority of hours in the year
insights.locator: In her view, the real bottleneck

insights.claim: Better load forecasting is named as one of the grid's core unmet needs, implying that current utility and RTO demand projections are not reliable enough to underwrite multi-billion-dollar build decisions.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Forecast quality is becoming a regulatory battleground; filings that revise load projections downward would hit capacity-price and generation-equity assumptions.
insights.locator: faster interconnection, better load forecasting, clearer price signals

themes.theme: Interconnection speed as the real bottleneck

insights.claim: The binding constraint on serving new large loads is not an absolute lack of power but the failure to connect those loads to the grid quickly enough, compounded by delays in transmission, distribution and interconnection processes.
insights.speaker: Stacey Doré, Vistra
insights.so_what: Directs capital and policy attention to process and queue reform rather than megawatt additions; interconnection-services and grid-equipment names benefit either way.
insights.quote: the real bottleneck is not an absolute lack of power, but the failure to connect new load to the grid quickly enough
insights.locator: In her view, the real bottleneck

insights.claim: Requiring every new large load to wait for one-for-one new generation before connecting is the wrong near-term policy, because it stalls revenue-generating demand while the system has spare hours available.
insights.speaker: Stacey Doré, Vistra
insights.so_what: Directly opposes bring-your-own-generation rules being debated in several states; the outcome determines how fast data-centre load monetises for IPPs.
insights.quote: the better near-term solution is not to force every new large load to wait for one-for-one new generation
insights.locator: She argues that the better near-term solution

insights.claim: The proposed alternative stack for managing the system is to connect customers faster, use co-location where possible, and lean on demand flexibility, backup generation and storage to cover the system's few genuine peak-stress hours.
insights.speaker: Stacey Doré, Vistra
insights.so_what: A concrete four-part playbook: flexibility, co-location and storage capture the value that would otherwise go to new peaking capacity.
insights.quote: connect customers faster, use co-location where possible, and rely on demand flexibility, backup generation and storage to manage the system’s few true peak-stress hours
insights.locator: She argues that the better near-term solution

themes.theme: Do competitive markets still send the right signals

insights.claim: Rising capacity and energy prices in PJM are cited as evidence that competitive wholesale markets are correctly signalling scarcity and pulling forward investment, rather than as evidence of market failure.
insights.speaker: Stacey Doré, Vistra
insights.so_what: The same PJM price spike is read by critics as consumer harm and by incumbents as a working signal; which reading wins decides whether PJM market design gets re-regulated.
insights.locator: Are competitive markets sending the right signals

insights.claim: Bilateral contracts struck directly with large customers, alongside a wave of announced investment in new and upgraded generation, are offered as proof that the competitive model is already delivering supply response.
insights.speaker: Stacey Doré, Vistra
insights.so_what: Bilateral large-load contracts move IPP revenue off merchant spot exposure toward contracted cash flows, which supports valuation multiples.
insights.locator: pointing to rising capacity and energy prices in PJM, bilateral contracts with large customers

insights.claim: In PJM and ERCOT, market design has stopped being an arcane technical debate and has become a live political question about whether competitive markets can still deliver affordable, reliable electricity during rapid growth.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Politicisation raises the probability of abrupt rule changes; merchant generator exposure to PJM and ERCOT now carries political rather than purely commercial risk.
insights.quote: those tensions are turning an arcane debate about market design into a live political question
insights.locator: In markets such as PJM and ERCOT

insights.claim: Clearer price signals are listed as a still-unmet requirement of the grid, implying that even defenders of competitive markets concede current signals are not fully doing their job.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Signals a middle path in the deregulation fight: market-design tweaks rather than wholesale re-regulation.
insights.locator: What emerges is less a simple argument for or against deregulation

themes.theme: Who pays: cost allocation and the bill stack

insights.claim: The rapidly rising component of consumer electricity bills is the transmission and distribution portion, not wholesale generation costs, which separates the affordability debate from the wholesale market-design debate.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: If T&D is the driver, re-regulating generation markets will not fix bills; regulated wires utilities are where the political pressure and rate-case risk actually land.
insights.quote: the distinction between wholesale generation costs and the rapidly rising transmission and distribution portion of electricity bills
insights.locator: The conversation digs into the distinction

insights.claim: Connecting more large industrial and data-centre loads to the grid spreads fixed system costs across a bigger base and therefore lowers the per-customer burden on households, making load growth an affordability tool rather than a threat.
insights.speaker: Stacey Doré, Vistra
insights.so_what: This is the industry's core political defence of data centres; its credibility depends on large loads paying their allocated share, which is exactly what is contested.
insights.locator: Stacey arguing that getting more large loads onto the grid

insights.claim: Cost allocation, not market structure, should be the first reform policymakers tackle if they want to protect residential customers while accommodating a new wave of industrial and data-centre demand.
insights.speaker: Amy Myers Jaffe
insights.so_what: Watch state and FERC cost-allocation dockets ahead of market-design proceedings; that is where large-load tariffs and household protections get decided.
insights.quote: cost allocation may be the first reform policymakers need to tackle
insights.locator: Amy counters that cost allocation may be the first reform

insights.claim: Even if competition works efficiently, the unresolved question is who bears the cost when prices rise and whether current cost-allocation rules are fair to households, a distributional issue that efficiency arguments do not answer.
insights.speaker: Amy Myers Jaffe
insights.so_what: Efficiency and fairness are separable; regulatory risk for generators comes from the fairness track even when the efficiency case is sound.
insights.quote: who pays when prices rise, and are current cost-allocation rules fair to households?
insights.locator: Amy pushes on the consumer side of the equation

insights.claim: Policymakers face three distinct forks: double down on competition, let regulated utilities build more rate-based generation, or rethink cost allocation altogether, and the choice determines who captures the returns from load growth.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A clean three-branch decision tree for positioning: branch two transfers value from merchant IPPs to regulated utility rate base.
insights.locator: Whether policymakers double down on competition

insights.claim: The stated stakes are keeping the grid reliable while bringing on new demand without pushing affordability further out of reach, framing reliability and affordability as a live trade-off rather than complements.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Where that trade-off is resolved politically sets the ceiling on allowed capacity prices and therefore on merchant generation margins.
insights.quote: keeping the grid reliable while bringing on new demand without pushing affordability further out of reach

insights.claim: Surging demand forecasts are colliding simultaneously with reliability anxiety, rising consumer bills and questions about the pace of new investment, so no single reform can satisfy all three constraints at once.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A trilemma framing: expect policy to trade one axis off explicitly, and position on whichever axis regulators sacrifice.
insights.locator: Electricity markets are under renewed pressure

insights.claim: Vistra has grown from a Texas utility successor into a multi-state owner of gas, nuclear, coal, solar and battery assets and is one of the largest competitive power producers and retailers in the US.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A fuel-diverse merchant fleet with retail attached is the structural winner if competitive markets survive intact and large loads connect faster.
insights.quote: one of the largest competitive power producers and retailers in the US
insights.locator: Host Ed Crooks and regular contributor Amy Myers Jaffe are joined by Stacey Doré

insights.claim: The case for competitive markets as the best mechanism for efficient investment, innovation and customer value is made by an executive whose company is among the largest beneficiaries of that structure, so the argument carries a clear incumbent interest.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Discount the forecast-deflation and connect-faster arguments accordingly; both conveniently reduce the obligation on merchant generators to build.
insights.locator: Stacey makes the case for competitive markets
